characterList.description: A person with their left hand, which has a ring on the ring finger, holding a pen and writing on a white paper sheet with small squares. On the left upper corner of the paper we see two blue horizontal lines above and below a black horizontal line and the words 'Area A' below the lowest blue line.
characterList.name: Lecturer

content_metadata.description: A lecture on the concept of viscosity, including its definition, calculation, and significance in fluid mechanics.

qAndA.answer: The lecturer says that the V in VPIGS is Viscous forces.
qAndA.question: What does the lecturer say is the V in VPIGS?

qAndA.answer: The lecturer draws six short horizontal lines between the two longer blue horizontal lines which represent the plates, connecting the top black line to the bottom blue line. These lines are evenly spaced and represent the linear velocity distribution of the fluid, where the fluid at the top is going the fastest and the fluid at the bottom is stationary.
qAndA.question: How does the lecturer draw the fluid between the plates?

qAndA.answer: The units for dynamic viscosity are Newton seconds per square meter.
qAndA.question: What are the units for dynamic viscosity?

qAndA.answer: The units for kinematic viscosity are meters squared per second.
qAndA.question: What are the units for kinematic viscosity?

qAndA.answer: The lecturer says that viscous forces are important either if the viscosity is large, or the gradients are large, or both.
qAndA.question: What does the lecturer say about the importance of viscous forces?

scenes.contextualRelevance: The scene establishes foundational knowledge about viscosity, which is critical for understanding fluid behavior in various contexts.

narrativeProgression.description: The lecturer defines viscosity as the V in VPIGS
The lecturer begins to draw a diagram of a fluid trapped between two plates
The lecturer describes how the plate on the top of the fluid pulls the fluid along at the same velocity
The lecturer describes how the plate at the bottom of the fluid holds it stationary
The lecturer describes how the force required to move the top plate changes with various factors
The lecturer creates an equation for the force required to move the top plate

The lecturer rearranges the equation to demonstrate that the force over the area, which will turn out to be a stress, is equal to mu, which has something to do with how thick the fluid is, times the ratio of the velocity to the gap size
The lecturer refines the equation further to express shear stress in terms of viscosity and velocity gradient
The lecturer defines the units for velocity gradient
The lecturer defines the units for shear stress
The lecturer defines the units for viscosity
The lecturer defines dynamic viscosity, which is represented with the Greek letter mu
The lecturer defines density, which is represented with the Greek letter rho
The lecturer defines kinematic viscosity, which is represented with the Greek letter nu, and is equal to the ratio of the dynamic viscosity to the density
The lecturer defines the units for kinematic viscosity
The lecturer clarifies that the shear stress is related to the velocity gradient by way of the constant of viscosity
The lecturer states that the viscous forces are important if either the viscosity is large, or the gradients are large, or both

trimmingSuggestions.description: The extended silent drawing of the diagram could be slightly shortened without sacrificing clarity.
The listing of factors affecting force required could be presented more concisely, perhaps with visual aids within the diagram.
The detailed explanation of units could be condensed, relying more on the written formulas for visual reinforcement.

Imagine for a moment that we've got a fluid in the middle here between two plates.
And one of these plates is moving up here at the top, at some velocity capital U,
and it will pull the fluid along with it at that same velocity capital U.
So that this piece of fluid right here is going that fast.
Down here at the bottom plate, it's not moving, so the fluid that's right adjacent to it will have no velocity,
so it'll only be going this fast.
And we'll wind up with a linear velocity distribution between these plates,
so that the stuff at the top is going fast and slower and slower.
We know this from inspection, from watching fluids behave,
and also to a little bit of an extent from intuition.
Now we can think of the gap between these two plates as some height H,
the thickness of this layer of fluid in between the two plates.
There's a surface area of the plates that's area A.
They're located in this coordinate frame of reference with Y going up and X going across as usual.
And this top plate pulls the fluid along at the same velocity.
This bottom plate holds the fluid stationary.
The force required to make this top plate move goes up with a variety of things,
and we know this from observation and from measurements.
It goes up with higher velocity, so that the faster we want to go,
the harder we're going to have to pull on that top plate.
It goes up with a smaller gap.
The thinner the gap in between these two plates, the harder it is going to be to pull the top one along.
It also goes up if we have a fluid that is thicker.
Let's just say thicker for the moment with quotation marks.
Different fluids will be easier or harder to deform this way.
And it also goes up as you'd expect with the surface area.
So the bigger the area of the plates, the harder you're going to have to pull to slide them along.
So if we write that as an equation, the force will be equal to, well, there's the area times the velocity,
that high U velocity, goes down with the thickness of the, or the height of the gap,
so divided by H, and then times something to do with the thickness of the fluid.

how thick the fluid is, times the ratio of the velocity and the gap size.

that's a velocity gradient.

is going to depend on this constant viscosity and the gradient of the velocity.
